text: Shinto, “the way of the kami”, is the native religion of Japan, with no founder and no single holy book.
In stories written down more than 1,300 years ago, the gods Izanagi and Izanami made the islands of Japan.
src: Shinto, “the way of the kami”, is the native religion of Japan / with no founder and no single scripture
the court commissioned the Kojiki in 712 and the Nihon Shoki in 720 / The myths of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki tell how the divine pair Izanagi and Izanami created the islands of Japan

text: Shinto believers worship the kami, sacred powers in mountains, trees, rivers, ancestors and great people.
People ask the kami for good harvests and health, and thank them at festivals called matsuri.
src: the worship of the kami, the sacred powers present in mountains, trees, rivers, ancestors and great people
People ask them for protection, good harvests, health, success and safe childbirth, and thank them in festivals, matsuri

text: Japan has some 80,000 shrines, holy places marked by a gateway called a torii.
Every twenty years the Grand Shrine of Ise is built again in the same form, on the site next to it.
src: Japan has some 80,000 Shinto shrines / A shrine is marked by a torii, a gateway
The Grand Shrine of Ise has been rebuilt in identical form on a neighbouring site every twenty years

text: For a thousand years, people in Japan worshipped the kami and the buddhas together.
From 1868 to 1945, Shinto was made the religion of the state, and the emperor was honoured as a living kami.
src: For a thousand years kami and buddhas were worshipped together
it was made the creed of the state from 1868 to 1945 / the emperor was revered as a living kami

text: The red gateway of the Itsukushima shrine rises from the sea.
Today most Japanese take part in Shinto festivals and New Year shrine visits, though few call it their religion.
src: the vermilion torii of Itsukushima rising from the sea
Most Japanese take part in its festivals and rites at some 80,000 shrines, though few call Shinto their religion / New Year shrine visits
